extracted.intended_audience: writers, students of literature, critics, and filmmakers interested in realism/verisimilitude in fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and conceptual dimensions for making a work of fiction feel believable—either relative to the real world or relative to its own genre/worldbuilding. Useful for writers, adapters, and critics evaluating plausibility and internal consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural verisimilitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Plausibility of the fictional work within the cultural and/or historical context of the real world, outside of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether events, behavior, and details are believable to readers given real-world cultural and historical knowledge. Example: actions that conflict with broadly held real-world facts will harm cultural verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic verisimilitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Plausibility of a fictional work within the bounds of its own genre (so that, for example, characters regularly singing about their feelings is a believable action within the fictional universe of a musical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge plausibility using genre conventions and expectations rather than real-world likelihood. What is credible in one genre (fantasy, musical, superhero) may be implausible in another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounding in reality / mimesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea, rooted in Platonic and Aristotelian mimesis, that a work of art must have grounding in reality — an imitation or representation of nature — for significance or persuasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use believable particulars and representations of human experience to lend the work weight and persuade an audience. Historically linked to making fiction instructive and pleasurable by reflecting realistic aspects of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorum (appropriate style and voice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The realistic union of style and subject: poetic/language choices must be appropriate to the character's age, gender, race, social position, and situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mismatches between a character's voice and their attributes; ensure language and behavior suit who the character is and the context they occupy. Decorum supports credibility and avoids jarring the reader out of the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willing suspension of disbelief / credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A fictional text needs credibility to promote the reader's willingness to suspend disbelief; anything physically possible in the worldview of the reader or humanity's experience was defined as credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To secure reader buy-in, present events and characters in ways that align with the reader's expectations or the established rules of the story world. Use credible detail and consistent presentation to encourage suspension of disbelief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prefatory material and historical referencing to establish credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Early novelists added a preface or included references to known history within the text to state or imply credibility to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When audience knowledge varies, authors can use framing devices (prefaces, historical anchors, citations) or contextual references to bolster plausibility. This is a strategy to address differing reader background knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscuring artifice to preserve illusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may obscure the fiction or art of the novel to avoid destroying illusion—hiding the 'made up' attributes of the text so the novel reads as a seamless whole rather than distinct parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid metatextual signals or visible construction that call attention to artifice unless intentionally breaking illusion. Anti-pattern: over-explaining mechanisms of the narrative in ways that remind readers they are reading fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal logic and structural verisimilitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Verisimilitude as a technical problem within the fictional world: the novel as a closed fictional world that establishes its own rules and laws, with detail centered on creating a logical cause web that reinforces plot structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure causal coherence, consistent rules, and logical relationships among events and character motivations within the story world. Inconsistencies in the cause–effect web or rule-breaking without explanation undermine internal verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of variable reader knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that readers differ in their real-world knowledge, so credibility cannot rely solely on assumed shared knowledge; strategies were used (prefaces, references, or internal consistency) to address this dilemma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate gaps in audience background and provide sufficient context or internal justification. Excess reliance on obscure real-world facts without context can break plausibility for some readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligibility precedes verisimilitude (postmodern perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: In some postmodern views, the reader first tests whether the novel works as an intelligible narrative; verisimilitude is applied only after the novel makes sense — truth/significance may lie beyond verisimilitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize narrative clarity and coherence of storytelling; only then assess realism. Some works intentionally deprioritize verisimilitude to challenge constructions of reality, allowing art to 'precede' reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity to source material as a means of internal credibility (adaptation practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Staying true to source material and approaching fantasy elements 'in a way true to the source material' can make a story feel intuitively real to an audience within the context of the story's world (example: Richard Donner on Superman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting or working within preexisting material, preserve the tonal and structural truths of the source to maintain audience sense of authenticity within the fictional world. Deviations that violate core truths of the source may harm perceived verisimilitude.
